Chapter 2: Building Genuine Interest—the Key to Influencing Others.
Once you've wrapped your head around what really motivates people, the next step is simple, but so powerful—cultivate a sincere interest in others. And I’m not talking about fake flattery or trying to manipulate someone.
This is about letting yourself get genuinely curious and appreciative of the people you meet every day.
Picture a garden for a second. Each plant needs something a little different—some want bright sunlight, some thrive in the shade. People are the same way. Tailored attention is like that sunlight; it’s what helps relationships grow strong.
Now, in theory, this sounds easy. But in practice? It’s a game-changer. When you show someone you care—not just about what they do, but about who they are and what they experience—they’re way more likely to open up and respond positively. You get this wonderful cycle of trust and cooperation going.
So, how do you actually do this? Here are a few tried-and-true tips:
First, remember people’s names and use them. A name is more than just a word—it’s part of who someone is. Using it with care shows you respect them and you’re paying attention.
Second, ask about their interests, their work, their family. Little things, like remembering their favorite hobby, show that their life matters to you.
And third, listen. I mean really listen—don’t interrupt, don’t rush to jump in with your own story. Giving someone your full attention is one of the most valuable gifts you can offer.
Let’s make this real. Imagine you’re a salesperson meeting a new client. Instead of launching straight into your pitch, you start by asking about their business, their biggest challenges. Then, you just listen. Not only do you learn what matters to them, but you’re also building trust—and that makes them far more open to what you have to say.
Here’s the thing: you can’t fake genuine interest. People are surprisingly good at picking up on insincerity. The goal isn’t to collect personal details for your own benefit—it’s to make a habit of curiosity and appreciation. Over time, this changes how you connect with people. Relationships become deeper, more rewarding, and much more resilient.
And this isn’t just for good times. When you’re in conflict or at odds with someone, taking a moment to understand what matters to them—what they care about, or even what scares them—can break the ice and make it easier to find common ground.
So, if you remember one thing from this, let it be this: building genuine interest means shifting your focus away from yourself and tuning in to others. It’s a quiet, powerful way to influence people—not by pushing or persuading, but by making them feel truly seen and valued.
